title: De Liturgia Gallicana Libri Tres
author: Germanus Parisiensis Episcopus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1224.tmp1224.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Post ipsam dicitur, Pax vobiscum, et osculanturse Christiani in osculo sancto. » Denique cum in Ordine Mozarabico semper duae lectiones ante Evangelium , una ex Veteri Testamento, alia ex Novo praemittatur; unica erat in Africano , teste Augustino in sermone 7 de verbis Apostoli : < Apostolum audivimus, psalmum audivimus, Evangelium audivimus : consonant omnes divinae lectio- Des. » Idem clarius habetur in sermone 10 de verbis Apostoli, et in sermone 33 de verbis Domini secundum Lucam, et alibi.
passages.english: "After it 'Peace be with you' is said, and the Christians kiss one another with a holy kiss." Finally, whereas in the Mozarabic Order two readings are always placed before the Gospel, one from the Old Testament and the other from the New, in the African [Order] there was only one, as Augustine testifies in sermon 7 on the words of the Apostle: "We have heard the Apostle, we have heard the psalm, we have heard the Gospel: all the divine readings agree." The same is found more clearly in sermon 10 on the words of the Apostle, and in sermon 33 on the words of the Lord according to Luke, and elsewhere.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'osculanturse' = osculantur se; 'lectio- Des' = lectiones.

passages.original: Quo nomine veteres passim sacra 29 Eucharistiæ mysteria designabant. Hine Yoconius, Castellani in Mauritania episcopus, apud eumdem Gennadium composuisse dicitur volumen Sacramentorum. Quo modo Augustinus sacramenta vocat Dominicæ mensæ sacrificium, ex dictis.
passages.english: By this name the ancients commonly designated the sacred mysteries of the Eucharist. Hence Voconius, bishop of Castellum in Mauretania, is said by the same Gennadius to have composed a volume of Sacraments. In the same way Augustine calls the sacrifice of the Lord's table 'sacraments', as follows from what has been said.
passages.notes: 'Hine Yoconius' read as 'Hinc Voconius'. 'Castellani' taken as the see of Castellum in Mauretania.

passages.original: 6. Sed et ante Musaeum Hilarius, Pictavorum sanctissimus antistes, librum Hymnorum, et alium Mysteriorum scripsit, auctore Hieronymo in libro de Scriptoribus cap. 100. Hymnus Gloria in excelsis ab eodem auctus et consummatus dicitur in vulgato Atcuino. His duobus merito annumerandus est Sidonius Arvenorum episcopus, cujus libro de Missis ab eo compositis Gregorius Turonensis præfationem adjunxit, ex lib.
passages.english: 6. But even before Musaeus, Hilary, the most holy bishop of Poitiers, wrote a book of Hymns and another of Mysteries, on the authority of Jerome in the book On Writers, chapter 100. The hymn Gloria in excelsis is said in the published Alcuin to have been enlarged and completed by the same [Hilary]. To these two Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, is rightly to be added, to whose book of Masses composed by him Gregory of Tours added a preface, according to book
passages.notes: 'Atcuino' read as 'Alcuino'. The sentence breaks off; the reference continues in the following passage (II Histories, ch. 22).

passages.original: 7. Tales auctores, id est Hilarium, Musæum, et Sidonium, habuisse videiur Ordo missae Gallicanus, quem a Romano diversum exeunte saeculo vi fuisse constat ex epistola Gregorii magni ad Augustinum : qui tertio loco Gregorium interrogavit, < cur cum una sit fides , diversae sint Ecclesiarum consuetudines; et altera consuetudo missarum in Romana ecclesia, atque altera in Galliarum Ecclesiis teneatur.
passages.english: 7. The Gallican Order of Mass seems to have had such authors, that is, Hilary, Musaeus and Sidonius; and that it was different from the Roman at the end of the sixth century is established from the letter of Gregory the Great to Augustine, who in the third place asked Gregory "why, since the faith is one, the customs of the Churches are different, and one custom of Masses is kept in the Roman church and another in the Churches of the Gauls."

passages.original: Porro missa expleta censebatur ante commonionem, ut docet Gregorius Turonensis antistes in lib. II de Miraculis sancti Martini, cap. 47 : « Cumque expletis missis, populus cœpisset sacrosanctum corpus Redemptoris accipere, # etc. Cyprianus ad eum fere modum 36 loquitur in libro de LapsiS : « Ubi vero, solomnibus adimpletiS, calicem diaconus offerre præsentibus coepit, » etc. Quantum porro duraret saecuo VI missae celebratio, declarat Cæsarius in utro- que setmone prælandato, ubi ait, divina mysteria « unius vel duarum horarum spatio > peracta fuisse.
passages.english: Moreover, the Mass was considered completed before communion, as Bishop Gregory of Tours teaches in book II of the Miracles of Saint Martin, chapter 47: "And when, the Masses having been completed, the people had begun to receive the most holy body of the Redeemer," etc. Cyprian speaks in almost the same way in the book On the Lapsed: "But when, the solemnities having been fulfilled, the deacon began to offer the cup to those present," etc. How long, further, the celebration of Mass lasted in the sixth century is shown by Caesarius in both sermons cited above, where he says that the divine mysteries were performed "in the space of one or two hours."

passages.original: Nihil porro hac de re In Missalibus Gallicanis praescribitur : sed orationi, quae post mysterium seu post consecrationem assignatur, continuo alia subjicitur Praefationis instar ante orationem Dominicalem, et varia quidem in singulis fere missis. Sic in Natali Domini : Non nostro præsumentes, Pater sancte, merito, sed Domini nostri Jesu Christi obedientes imperio, audemus dicere : Pater noster, etc. De hoc universali more Hieronymus ita scribit in lib. III contra Pelagium : < Sic docuit apostolos suos, ut quotidie in corporis sui sacrificio credentes audeant loqui : Pater noster qui es in cælis.
passages.english: Furthermore, nothing is prescribed on this matter in the Gallican Missals; but to the prayer which is assigned after the mystery, that is, after the consecration, another is immediately added, in the manner of a Preface, before the Lord's Prayer, and indeed it varies in almost every single mass. Thus on the Nativity of the Lord: "Not presuming on our own merit, holy Father, but obeying the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, we dare to say: Our Father, etc." Of this universal custom Jerome writes thus in Book III against Pelagius: "He so taught his apostles that daily, as believers, in the sacrifice of his body they should dare to say: Our Father, who art in heaven.
passages.notes: The quotation from Jerome opens but does not close within the passage.

passages.original: 27. Quid tempore communionis apud Gallos caneretur, videndum. Psalmi cantabantur in Carthaginensi seu Africana ecclesia, teste Augustino, cujus tempore id fieri cæptum. > Inter hæc (ut ipse ait in lib. II Retractationum cap. 11) Hilarus quidam, vir tribunitius, laicus catholicus, nescio unde adversus Dei ministros, ut fieri assolet, irritatus, morem qui tunc esse apud Carthaginem coeperat, ut hymni ad allare dicerentur de Psalmorum libro, sive ante oblationem, sive cum distribueretur populo quod fuisset oblalum, maledica reprehensione, ubicunque poterat, lacerabat, asserens fieri non oportere.
passages.english: 27. We must see what was sung among the Gauls at the time of communion. Psalms were sung in the church of Carthage, or Africa, as Augustine testifies, in whose time this began to be done. "Meanwhile," as he himself says in book II of the Retractations, chapter 11, "a certain Hilarus, a man of tribunician rank, a Catholic layman, angered for some reason against the ministers of God, as commonly happens, was assailing with abusive censure, wherever he could, the custom which had then begun at Carthage, that hymns from the book of Psalms should be said at the altar, either before the offering or while what had been offered was being distributed to the people, asserting that it ought not to be done."

passages.original: Odo abbas Cluniacensis singulare lactum cujusdam presbyteri Turonensis refert, qui, sancti Andreae festo eum Dominica prima Adventus concurrente, < pagensibus suis utrasque missas audire praecepit. > Lo- I cum adeat qui volet in Collationum lib. i cap. ii. Redeo ad missas Quadragesimae et Rogationum, quibus recte aptari potest quod de stationibus ait Tertullianus sub finem libri de Oratione : < Nonne solemnior erit statio tua, si ad aram Dei steteris? > Certe saeculo IX apud nostrates a missis quadragesimalibus abesse religio erat, ex lib. n de Miraculis sancti Dionysii cap. 35.
passages.english: Odo, abbot of Cluny, relates a singular deed of a certain priest of Tours who, when the feast of Saint Andrew coincided with the first Sunday of Advent, "ordered his country people to hear both Masses." Whoever wishes may consult the passage in the Collations, book I, chapter 2. I return to the Masses of Lent and of the Rogations, to which one may rightly apply what Tertullian says about stations near the end of the book On Prayer: "Will not your station be more solemn if you have stood at the altar of God?" Certainly in the ninth century among our people it was considered a matter of conscience not to be absent from the Lenten Masses, according to book II of the Miracles of Saint Denis, chapter 35.
passages.notes: 'lactum' read as 'factum'; 'lib. n' as 'lib. II'. Chapter numbers in the Collations reference ('i', 'ii') are uncertain in the scan.

passages.original: Erat proinde capsa illud genus indumenti, quod modo cappam appellamus, cujus pars 63 posterior ex humeris dependens pro cucullo quondam erat ad caput operiendum, qualis est cappa sancti Audomari episcopi, in sancti Bertini monasterio hactenus asserta. Casulam processoriam vocat Cyprianus episcopus Tolonensis in lib. i de Vita Cæsarii episcopi Arelatensis, num. 23, qui hanc casulam < albamque paschalem », pauperi cuidam largitus est.
passages.english: The capsa, then, was that kind of garment which we now call the cope, whose rear part, hanging from the shoulders, once served as a hood to cover the head; such is the cope of Saint Audomar, bishop, preserved to this day in the monastery of Saint Bertin. Cyprian, bishop of Toulon, in book I of the Life of Caesarius, bishop of Arles, no. 23, calls it a processional chasuble; [Caesarius] gave this chasuble "and his paschal alb" to a certain poor man.

passages.original: Tum interpositis quibusdam ejusdem pontificis sententiis gravissimis : < Non credo, ait (Vir sanctus) contrarium esse Deo, de ministerio suo redemptionem dari, qui se ipsum pro hominis redemptione tradidit. » Cumque ejus factum alii culparent, probarent vero alii, subdit Cyprianus episcopus qui hæc refert in lib. i de Cæsarii Vita num. i i : < Nonne in vitro sanguis Christi, et in ligno corpus pretiosissimum ejus pependit pro nobis et fulsit ? > Quæ sententia Hieronymi dictum in memoriam revocat ex epistola ad Rusticum, ubi de Exuperio Tolosae episcopo, qui < omnem substantiam Christi visceribus erogavit, > atque 65 indubie vasa sacra, propter verba quæ sequuutur : < Nihil illo ditius, qui corpus Domini in canistro vimineo, sanguinem portat in vitro.
passages.english: Then, after inserting some very weighty sayings of the same bishop: "I do not believe," says the holy man, "that it is contrary to God that redemption be given from his own ministry, since he gave himself up for the redemption of man." And when some blamed his deed while others approved it, Bishop Cyprian, who reports these things in book I of the Life of Caesarius, no. 11, adds: "Did not the blood of Christ hang in glass, and his most precious body on wood, for us, and shine?" This saying recalls a remark of Jerome in the letter to Rusticus, concerning Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, who "spent his whole substance on the bowels of Christ," and undoubtedly the sacred vessels, because of the words that follow: "No one is richer than he who carries the body of the Lord in a wicker basket and the blood in glass."
passages.notes: 'num. i i' may be 11 or a misread number. 'visceribus' = the poor, Christ's 'bowels' (inmost members).

passages.original: Porro cancelli aliquando, vel saltem eorum ornamenta, constabant argento, cui non pepercit 78 Caesarius episcopus Arelatensis, illud expendens in captivorum redemptionem. « Videntur etiam hodieque (ait Cyprianus in lib. I de ejus Vita, num. 17) securium ictus in pediis et cancellis, dum inde columnarilm ex argent excutiuntur ornamenta. »
passages.english: Moreover, the chancel screens, or at least their ornaments, were sometimes made of silver, which Caesarius, bishop of Arles, did not spare, spending it on the redemption of captives. "Even today," says Cyprian in book I of his Life, no. 17, "the blows of axes are seen on the pedestals and screens, where the silver ornaments of the columns were struck off them."

passages.original: Sacrarium locus est altaris, quem locum vela ad ostia presbyterii appensa tegebant. Inferiorum vero ministrorum id officii erat, ut senioribus vela ad ostis sublvarent, ex concilii Narbonensis canone 13. Nepotianus, teste Hieronymo, maxime sollicitus erat, « si niteret altare, si parietes absque fuligine, si pavimentum tersum, si janitor creber in porta, si vela semper in ostiis, si sacrarium mundum, si vasa luculenta, et in omnes caeremonias pia sollicitudo disposita. » Ad haec in ciboriis etam vela quatuor, ne sacra quorumvis aspectui paterent, suspensa fuisse colligi potest ei simili more non solum Græcorum, sed etiam Romanorum, de quibus Anastasius io Leone III : « Fecit et in circuitu altaris alia vela alba, holoserica rosata, quae pendent in arcu de ciborio, numero quatuor.
passages.english: The sanctuary (*sacrarium*) is the place of the altar, a place which veils hung at the entrances of the presbytery used to cover. It was the duty of the lower ministers to raise the veils at the entrances for the elders, according to canon 13 of the Council of Narbonne. Nepotian, as Jerome attests, was especially concerned "whether the altar shone, whether the walls were free of soot, whether the floor was swept, whether the doorkeeper was constantly at the door, whether the veils were always at the entrances, whether the sanctuary was clean, whether the vessels were gleaming, and [whether] a devout care was directed to all the ceremonies." In addition, it can be inferred that four veils were also hung on the ciboria, so that the sacred things should not lie open to the gaze of just anyone, after the similar custom not only of the Greeks but also of the Romans, concerning whom Anastasius [says] in [the life of] Leo III: "He also made around the altar other veils, white, of pure silk, rose-coloured, which hang on the arch of the ciborium, four in number.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'ostis sublvarent' read as 'ostia sublevarent'; 'etam' as 'etiam'; 'ei simili' as 'ex simili'; 'io Leone' as 'in Leone'. The sense of 'senioribus' (elders, i.e. presbyters or senior clergy) is uncertain.

passages.original: 559, apud Goarem : < His dictis, » scilicet post baptismum, et unctionem baptizatis impertitam, < patriarcha ingreditur cum recenter illuminatis ad Introitum, et deinceps divinam perficii miSSam, ϰαὶ τελεῑ ὰϰολουθω̄ς τὴν θείαν λειτουργίαν. » Unde consequens est, sacrum Christi sanguinem ex præcedenti sacrificio fuisse reservatum. Quod etiaM de aha Eucharistiæ specie satis innuit Chrysostomus, ubi ait irrupisse ubi sacra erant reposita, et vidisse omnia quæ intus erant. Denique verbum ὰπέϰειντο idem est ac repositum, reservatum ad tempus. Hanc reservationem improbarunt quidam sæculo IV, putantes < mysticam benedictionem nihil ad sanctificationem proficere, si quid ex ea fiat reliqui in alium diem, > quos < insanire > dicit Cyrillus Alexandrinus ad Calosyrium episcopum scribens.
passages.english: 559, in Goar: "When these things had been said," that is, after baptism and the anointing bestowed on the baptized, "the patriarch enters with the newly illuminated for the Introit, and then performs the divine mass, and celebrates the divine liturgy in order (kai telei akolouthōs tēn theian leitourgian)." From which it follows that the sacred blood of Christ had been reserved from a preceding sacrifice. That this was also the case with the other species of the Eucharist Chrysostom indicates clearly enough, where he says that they burst into the place where the sacred things had been laid up, and saw everything that was inside. Finally, the word apekeinto is the same as "laid up," "reserved for a time." Certain people in the fourth century disapproved of this reservation, thinking "that the mystical blessing contributes nothing to sanctification if any of it is left over for another day"; these Cyril of Alexandria, writing to Bishop Calosyrius, says are "insane."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-reference ("pag. 559" from the preceding context, i.e. page 559 of Goar's Euchologion). Scanning errors corrected: perficii > perficit, aha > alia; Greek accents garbled in the scan. "Mass" here renders Latin missam glossing the Greek leitourgia.

passages.original: In Quadragesima non una erat de missis ferialibus et quotidianis apud Latinos disciplina. In quibusdam quotidie, in aliis tantum certis diebus fiebat sacrificium, testante Augustino in epistola ad Januarinm. In ecclesia Mediolanensi videtur usus fuisse Sacrificii quotidiani. Insignis est in eam rem Ambrosii locus in sermone octavo super psalmum 126 CXVIII ad versum 6 : « Indictum est jejunium ;
passages.english: In Lent the discipline regarding ferial and daily Masses was not uniform among the Latins. In some [churches] the sacrifice was offered daily, in others only on certain days, as Augustine attests in his letter to Januarius. In the church of Milan the practice of a daily Sacrifice seems to have existed. There is a notable passage of Ambrose on this matter in the eighth sermon on Psalm 118, at verse 6: "A fast has been proclaimed;
passages.notes: '126' before 'CXVIII' appears to be a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted. 'Januarinm' read as 'Januarium'.

passages.original: Nullum bic officium praescribitur pro vigilia Pentecostes. An repetendum ex vigilia Paschae' Certe vigilia Pentecostes in Mozarabico notatur ad Nonam. Quod jejunii indicium est, cujus tamen nullum apud Isidorum vestigium invenio. Certe neque apud Ambrosium in sermone 60. Neque enim Ambrosii videtur esse sermo ille, cujus fragmentum refertur dist. 76, cap. 9, ubi auctor festum Pentecostes cum Paschate comparando, ait in vigiliis utriusque fuisse jejunatum : < Tunc enim, 157 sicut modo fecimus, jejunavimus Sabbato, Vigilias celebravimus, orationibus pernoctantes institimus.
passages.english: No office is prescribed here for the vigil of Pentecost. Is it to be taken over from the vigil of Easter? Certainly the vigil of Pentecost is noted in the Mozarabic [book] at None. This is a sign of fasting, yet I find no trace of it in Isidore. Certainly not in Ambrose either, in sermon 60. For that sermon does not seem to be Ambrose's, of which a fragment is cited in distinction 76, chapter 9, where the author, comparing the feast of Pentecost with Easter, says that there was fasting on the vigils of both: "For then, just as we have now done, we fasted on the Saturday, we celebrated the Vigils, we persevered through the night in prayers.
passages.notes: 'bic' read as 'hic'. '157' is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted. 'dist. 76, cap. 9' presumably refers to Gratian's Decretum.

passages.original: Extra Quadragesimam Alleluia saepius repetitur in Introitu, et post Evangelium. Deinde ad oblationem dicitur Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison, praeter morem. Gregorius, in Historiae lib. ivcap. 31, Catonem presbyterum Arvernum laudat, qui lue ingruente < populum sepelierat, et missas viriliter dixerat. i Idem, in lib. de Gloria confessorum, cap. 65, agit de muliere, quae, mortuo marito suo, < per annum integrum celebrans quotidie missarum solemuia, offerebat oblationem pro memoria viri, non diffisa de Domini misericordia, quod haberet defunctus requiem in die, qua Domino oblationem 165 pro ejus anima delibasset.
passages.english: Outside Lent the Alleluia is repeated more often in the Introit and after the Gospel. Then at the offering 'Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison' is said, contrary to custom. Gregory, in book 4, chapter 31 of the History, praises Cato, a priest of Clermont (Arverni), who, when the plague struck, "had buried the people and had boldly said Masses." The same [author], in the book On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 65, treats of a woman who, after her husband died, "celebrating the solemnities of Masses daily for a whole year, offered the oblation for her husband's memory, not distrusting the Lord's mercy that the departed would have rest on the day on which she had offered the oblation to the Lord for his soul.
passages.notes: 'ivcap.' read as 'iv cap.'; 'solemuia' as 'solemnia'; '165' is a printed page number and is omitted.
